headline: DeltaPulse Bot Open-Sourced for $500/Day Momentum Trading
summary: A developer has open-sourced a complete Polymarket trading bot, offering a full vertical slice from wallet to frontend for developers to study or fork.
details: A developer has open-sourced DeltaPulse Bot, a momentum-driven Polymarket trading bot designed to generate up to $500 per day. This project provides a comprehensive, production-shaped codebase for developers interested in prediction market tooling.

The bot includes a full vertical slice of components: wallet flow, on-chain logic, backend state management, and a responsive frontend. This allows developers to study, fork, or build upon the existing structure.

The project is available on GitHub, with a detailed README providing instructions for environment variables, deployment scripts, and testing commands. Issues and pull requests are welcomed by the developer.

This open-source release aims to help developers learn and contribute to the growing field of prediction market tooling. The developer encourages users to star the GitHub repository to increase its visibility.

topic: rare medical case: man with worms mistaken for brain cancer
headline_marked: Doctors [[mistook brain worms for cancer]] after patient's persistent headaches
headline: Doctors mistook brain worms for cancer after patient's persistent headaches
summary: A man's persistent headaches and behavioral changes led doctors to suspect brain cancer, but advanced imaging revealed parasitic tapeworm larvae.
details: A 60-year-old man in Spain presented with a two-week history of worsening headaches and subtle behavioral changes. Initial neurological exams showed mild motor delays, and blood work revealed elevated IgE levels, a marker for parasitic infections.

A CT scan of his head showed multiple lesions and swelling, leading doctors to suspect metastatic cancer. He was treated with anti-inflammatory corticosteroids for symptom relief while undergoing extensive tests, including full-body CT, colonoscopy, and PET/CT scans, none of which revealed malignancies.

Further examination with an MRI scan provided clearer images, revealing that the lesions were not tumors but encapsulated tapeworm larvae, specifically visible as 'scolexes' (worm heads). This diagnosis, neurocysticercosis (NCC), was surprising given the parasite is not endemic to Spain.

Doctors theorized the infection may have stemmed from his previous work in construction, where he was exposed to individuals from regions where pork tapeworms (Taenia solium) are common. The parasite spreads via the fecal-oral route, and he may have been exposed through shared meals or bathrooms with an infected coworker.

Taenia solium infections occur by consuming undercooked meat with cysts or ingesting eggs through fecal contamination. When eggs reach the central nervous system, they form larvae called cysticerci, leading to NCC. The severity of NCC depends on the location of the larvae in the brain.

Fortunately, the man's infection caused relatively mild symptoms. After testing confirmed antibodies against Taenia solium, doctors prescribed anti-parasitic drugs, leading to his recovery. The case highlights that travel history isn't always a prerequisite for diagnosing NCC.
